signal.title: core/telemetry: tolerate missing caller metadata
signal.text: `parseCallerCalleeRefs` is best-effort span enrichment, but it read `cm.Labels` straight off the client metadata — and that metadata is nil whenever `MainClientCallerMetadata` fails. That is the same discarded-error path that made a nil served-deps builder crash `SchemaBuilder.Lookup`: the error is dropped, the nil flows on, and something that exists purely to decorate a span takes down the engine instead. Read the labels through a local map so absent metadata means "no labels" and the call degrades to no refs, which is what best-effort enrichment should do. `core/telemetry_test.go` covers both nil client-scoped lookups — each of which panicked before this change and the `Lookup` guard. --- This is one half of a pair. #13913 guards the nil receiver in `SchemaBuilder.Lookup`; the tests here exercise both crashes, so reviewing them together is easiest. They touch disjoint files and can land in either order. Independent bug fix, based on `main`. Extracted from the LLM workspace stack (#13832–#13838); it has no dependency on those PRs and can land on its own.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: core: make SchemaBuilder.Lookup nil-safe
signal.text: `SchemaBuilder.Lookup` dereferenced its receiver unconditionally, but the builder that reaches it can legitimately be nil. `CurrentServedDeps` returns `(nil, err)` once the calling client's session is gone, and `parseCallerCalleeRefs` discards that error before calling `Lookup`. So a module call issued from an agent's tool loop — where sessions come and go underneath long-running work — could crash the whole engine from telemetry span enrichment alone. Nothing about the call itself was wrong; the panic came from decorating it. Guard the nil receiver the way `Mods()` already does, so a nil builder simply resolves nothing and the enrichment degrades to "no refs". Three lines in `core/moddeps.go`. --- This is one half of a pair. #13914 fixes the other nil dereference reachable from the same discarded-error path (`cm.Labels` off nil client metadata) and carries the regression tests that exercise both crashes. Independent bug fix, based on `main`. Extracted from the LLM workspace stack (#13832–#13838); it has no dependency on those PRs and can land on its own.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: TUI: keep notification and flowing output stable
signal.text: Four related fixes for one class of bug: content that occupies more terminal rows than the renderer thinks it does, which corrupts everything painted after it. **The invariant.** tuist treats every `ctx.Line` entry as exactly one terminal row — overlay height, viewport clipping and the diff renderer's relative cursor moves are all counted in slice elements. An entry that occupies two rows makes `hardwareCursorRow` a lie from that frame on, so subsequent updates land one row off and duplicate or clobber unrelated lines across the screen. **Notification bubbles broke it.** `NotificationBubble` padded each content line with `lipgloss.NewStyle().Width(innerWidth).Render()`, and lipgloss v2's `Width` does not truncate — `Style.Render` calls `Wrap` → `ansi.Wrap`, which word-wraps and hard-breaks long words. A long host path from the References section, or an unbounded error string, came back as a multi-row string handed to a single `ctx.Line`. tuist's own width clamp doesn't catch it either, because `ansi.Truncate` measures `"\n"` as zero width and preserves it — which is why the corrupted rows ended in a stray character from the wrapped remainder instead of the closing border. Each line is now clamped to the inner width with an ANSI-aware truncate before padding. **Zero-width cursor movers broke it too.** Vertical tab and form feed move the cursor down a row just like a line feed; a bare carriage return jumps to column 0 so the rest of the line overwrites what it already painted. All three measure as zero columns, so neither the bubble's clamp nor tuist's caught them. They're now dropped alongside the existing tab expansion, so the box's one-row-per-line guarantee holds for any content a producer hands it — not just over-long content. **Guarded at the framework level.** `go.mod` picks up the tuist row-count guard: `Context.Line`/`Context.Lines` split embedded newlines into separate rows at the source, and `renderFrame` expands tabs before measuring width and neutralizes surviving cursor-moving controls. A component emitting a multi-row string can no longer desynchronize the diff renderer at all. (Also pulls midterm to v0.2.5, which tuist bumped in the same merge to restore the `go-ansicode` Handler interface its `vt` package builds against.) **Flowing mode stops repainting history.** Flowing shell output enters native terminal scrollback, where mutating any old line forces a full synchronized frame repaint. Running rows now render with a stable marker and no elapsed duration in that mode, while viewport-clipped views keep their animated indicators. Tests cover the overlong-bubble case, pin the upstream lipgloss wrapping behavior the bubble must defend against, and assert that neither running conversation tools nor linked effects mount a ticker-backed child in flowing mode while completed error output stays unchanged. --- Independent fix, based on `main`. Extracted from the LLM workspace stack (#13832–#13838); it has no dependency on those PRs and can land on its own.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: engine/server: sweep discarded cache state in the background
signal.text: Resetting invalid local cache state — after an unclean shutdown, a schema mismatch, a corrupt DB — deleted the entire worker root directory inline with `os.RemoveAll` before the engine came up. On a warm cache that is tens of gigabytes across millions of inodes. Startup blocked for the whole delete, and the unlink storm saturated the disk queue hard enough to stutter the *host* for about a minute. The engine hadn't done anything yet; it was still taking out the trash. **Rename, then sweep.** The discarded state is moved aside to a sibling `worker-trash-<unique>` directory — an O(1) rename on the same filesystem — so startup proceeds immediately. A background sweeper then removes the tree at a bounded duty cycle: 50ms of unlinks, 200ms of rest, so the filesystem journal drains between bursts instead of being monopolized. The sweeper is not naive about it: - It runs at **full speed** when the disk is under the same free-space pressure that triggers cache GC — pacing is a courtesy, not a suicide pact. - Leftover trash dirs are **resumed on the next startup** if a sweep was interrupted, so nothing accumulates silently. - Stale mounts left behind by the crashed engine are **detached** rather than failing the reset (recursively up front, plus an `EBUSY` fallback per path). The unclean-shutdown integration test now polls the state volume until the trash dir is actually swept, so discarded state cannot quietly leak across resets. New: `engine/server/trash.go` and its unit tests. Changelog entry included. --- Independent fix, based on `main`. Extracted from the LLM workspace stack (#13832–#13838); it has no dependency on those PRs and can land on its own.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: LLM: fail turns cut short by refusal or output limit
signal.text: A provider can end a turn early — a safety refusal, an output-token ceiling, a truncated stream — and until now that mostly looked like success. Every provider client consulted the stop reason only when *no* content came back at all. A turn that streamed something and then stopped short fell through the empty-content guard and was handed to the agent loop as a normal response. An Anthropic refusal that fired a few thinking tokens first left exactly one truncated block: content was non-empty, the stop reason was discarded, and the loop saw a valid turn with no tool calls. It closed the turn and parked idle. No error anywhere — the agent just stopped, and the reason it stopped was thrown away one layer down. **The fix is ordering:** each client now checks the stop reason *before* it looks at content. The check is deliberately asymmetric, because the enums are: - **Anthropic** and **OpenAI** reject a known-bad list, so a stop reason the client has never heard of keeps working instead of failing a good turn. - **Gemini** allows a known-good list, since its enum is almost entirely failure modes and an empty reason just means the stream is still open. - The **Codex** client handled only `response.completed`; it now handles `response.incomplete` and `response.failed` too. A cut-short turn surfaces as a `ModelFinishedError` the user can actually see, rather than a silent idle. Recovery behavior is untouched — this only changes whether the failure is reported, not what happens next. `core/llm_stop_reason_test.go` covers each client's classification, including the unrecognized-reason path that must stay permissive. --- Independent bug fix, based on `main`. Extracted from the LLM workspace stack (#13832–#13838); it has no dependency on those PRs and can land on its own.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: dagger agent dev env: in-repo agent modules
signal.text: The dogfooding layer: the in-repo agent modules that `dagger agent --env dev` composes, plus the wiring that makes them reachable. No engine changes. | module | what it does | | --- | --- | | `editor` | a sandboxed coding agent — read, write, edit, find, grep, todoWrite — plus a commit tool built on the workspace's staged commits. Vendored from `github.com/vito/editor` so it can be iterated on in-tree. | | `review` | the `git status` / `git diff` an agent with no Bash tool can't otherwise get, via `Workspace.git.uncommitted`'s diffstats and patch | | `history` | the `git log` half of the same, over `Workspace.git.stagedCommits` | | `delegate` | hands a noisy, context-heavy subtask to a fresh sub-agent that runs it in its own conversation and returns one distilled report | | `engine-lab` | `./hack/dev` + `./hack/with-dev` as agent tools: build from the workspace, hold the engine as a Service, exec against it, poke its debug endpoints | | `contributor` | the same idea aimed at somebody else's repo — fetch it as a Workspace, compose editor's tools onto it, work the task, open the PR | | `tui-qa` | drives nested agent TUI sessions; now inherits the session's LLM config and gets a real git repo as its fixture | Supporting changes: `EngineDev.GoContainer` is a Wolfi Go base with the from-source `dagger` on `$PATH`, so Go commands (and the integration tests, which shell out to `dagger`) find the CLI without paying for a full engine build — it's what the `golang` toolchain is based on in the dev env. `dagger.toml` gains the `env.dev` module set, with contributor's GitHub token resolving through `cmd://gh auth token` rather than being stored. And catwalk moves to v0.51.11 for its refreshed model catalog. Each module commit is self-contained, and the `dagger.toml` wiring is last, so any intermediate state is a module directory with no install entry — inert rather than broken.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: Canonical host-git reconstruction from client packs
signal.text: The engine used to interpret a host checkout's raw git layout by hand — parsing gitfiles, chasing commondirs, stripping worktree plumbing, overriding config. That model produced two recurring failure classes: a **discovery landmine**, where a worktree or submodule `.git` pointer file synced into the engine points at a gitdir that doesn't exist there, so anything running near the tree dies with `fatal: not a git repository: (null)` (the Go SDK codegen's `git config` exec, for one); and a **layout interpreter** that had to keep growing to cover alternates, partial clones and separate git dirs. Invert it. Host git natively understands every checkout layout, so let the client's own git do the reading. Two new session RPCs: `CheckoutState` digests the checkout's ref state as a cache key that only changes when refs move, and `PackCheckout` streams a bundle of HEAD plus all branches and tags with the metadata needed to reconstruct a standalone repository engine-side. This is the mirror image of the `ApplyBundle` RPC that streams engine-staged commits the other way. `MaterializeHostGitCheckout` replaces a synced tree's `.git` with a canonical directory rebuilt from that pack — init, fetch, set HEAD, read-tree, pack-refs, strip mutable state — and the result is byte-identical for a given ref state regardless of how the host checkout is laid out. `Host.__gitDir` serves it keyed by state digest; `Workspace.git` pins to the workspace read epoch so a checkout that advances mid-session isn't silently re-read, preserving the staged-commit "local branch moved" guard; `ModuleSource.LoadContextGit` keys to live ref state. Separately, a root `.git` **pointer file** is dropped at load time for module contexts and workspace rootfs, since inside the engine it's dangling by construction. Plain `.git` directories are left alone and `Host.directory` semantics are untouched. With that, the hand-maintained layout model is deleted, along with the boundary-escaping "load any absolute host path" read it required. Coverage is the regression that motivated it — a Go SDK module whose `dagger.json` sits at a linked worktree's root now loads and runs — plus tree neutralization and plain-clone-versus-worktree parity. `hack/designs/host-git-reconstruction.md` records the as-built design, the error taxonomy, rejected alternatives with honest perf accounting, and the thin-pack follow-up.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: LLM continuations: tools that return a conversation
signal.text: Extends the tool-result state convention with one more ring: a tool that returns an LLM acts as a continuation. The agent loop resumes from the returned conversation — its env, tools, system prompts and history — instead of the one that made the call, so an agent can install a module or reload its own edited modules mid-conversation without restarting and losing context. A module function's `LLM!` argument is auto-filled with the conversation dispatching the tool call, exactly as a `Workspace!` argument is filled from the bound workspace, and hidden from the generated tool schema so the model never sees it. An `@agent`'s `base` stays required, since it's the composition entrypoint. Adoption mirrors the workspace convention rather than gating on lineage: the returned LLM's env and tools load eagerly so a broken module fails the tool call instead of bricking the next turn, at most one continuation is adopted per turn since LLMs don't merge the way Changesets do, and the swap is reported. A lineage check was tried and removed — it was inconsistent with `rebindWorkspace` accepting any workspace, it protected an env author from their own tools, and its first real use (editor's `reload`, which strips and re-adds system prompts) tripped it as a false positive. Protocol coherence replaces the gate's one real service. `step()` materializes the assistant response before dispatching tool calls, so the continuation is handed the conversation up to and including its own call, then appends the turn's tool results to the adopted LLM — degrading to a plain user message when the matching call ID isn't in the adopted history, since providers reject a `tool_result` with no matching `tool_use`. **The other half is making self-extension actually work.** An agent that edits its own modules and then recomposes itself couldn't see its own staged work, because module source and config were re-read from the on-disk checkout the session loaded at startup. Composition now re-resolves, through the overlay rootfs, every config entry the overlay affects. That alone wasn't enough: `LLM.tools` renders and dispatches against the served snapshot, so a replaced module showed stale docs and an overlay-installed one failed as "not an object in the workspace schema" — the served schema now layers the same overlay modules on, memoized so per-step derivation stays cheap.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: Engine-side git commit staging in Workspace
signal.text: Workspaces can now stage git commits the way they stage every other change: engine-side, building up until the user saves. Nothing touches the local checkout until `ctrl+s`, which lands the staged commits on the checked-out branch as a fast-forward. That leaves room for future sinks — push, submit-PR — that consume the same staged history with no local materialization. `Workspace.withCommit` folds the workspace's uncommitted changes, or only the given paths, into a commit on a persisted pending-commit stack. Afterwards `git.head` resolves to the staged HEAD and `git.uncommitted` shrinks to the remainder. The field is hermetic: the date is a required argument, author identity is captured once at workspace load, and nondeterministic `.git` scratch state is normalized, so the same workspace state and args always produce the same commit SHA. Callers wanting a wall-clock commit read `Query.currentTimestamp` and pass it in, which keeps the impurity in one small root field. Landing commits needs the client's own git, so the session git service gains `GetHead` and a streaming `ApplyBundle`. **Most of this PR is the four rounds of bugs that followed**, each found in a live session, and each the same shape: two different anchors disagreeing about what "uncommitted" means. 1. `withCommit` rewrote the overlay down to the uncommitted remainder — but for host workspaces that overlay is also what reconstructs the tree, so committing deleted content from reads, mounts and checks. Inverted around the invariant that committing moves content between layers without changing what the tree contains. 2. Pre-existing checkout dirt vanished on the first edit of a session, because a pristine workspace answered via the repository diff and an overlaid one via the overlay changeset, which is anchored on the already-dirty state. Anchors unified on the repository route. 3. Deleting a file whose only presence in staged HEAD came from a commit staged earlier in the same session was invisible, because the re-applied overlay was anchored pre-commit, where add-then-delete cancels out. Now applies the staged-anchored remainder. 4. Gitignored paths and paths inside a nested repo were invisible to status yet still written to the checkout on save — an agent could work in one all session, end with a clean status and uncommittable work, and have `ctrl+s` write it out unreviewed. Plus the fixes those turned up: `git apply` no longer dies during repository discovery inside a `git worktree` checkout (its `.git` names a gitdir that doesn't exist in the engine, which broke every changeset patch deterministically), `diff --git` headers are well-formed for added and deleted files, deleting the last file in a directory no longer emits a phantom directory stat, and a failed parallel changeset merge leaves conflict markers instead of discarding an entire batch of sub-agent work. The TUI Changes bubble renders the staged stack: uncommitted diffstats on top, then commits newest-first with their own dimmed diffstats. The final commit is a regen; per its message, only `sdk/go` and the GraphQL schema are actually this PR's new field, and the rest is pre-existing drift across the non-Go clients that regenerating necessarily picks up.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: Workspace cache volume mounts (DRAFT, unfinished)
signal.text: > [!WARNING] > **Draft — not ready to merge.** This is unfinished work that the layers above it are built on, so it's here to be reviewable and to keep the stack honest, not to land as-is. `Workspace.withMountedCache` mounts a cache volume at a path: it shadows base workspace content there, stays out of `Workspace.changes`, and commits into the volume on export. `withoutMount` removes it. A mount carries its own pending changeset, so reads and writes under it route to the mount's effective tree rather than the base overlay. Reads resolve through a deepest-match lookup, which gives shadowing for free while references keep priority in their reserved prefix. `search`, `glob` and `findUp` union the base with each mount, shadowing the base subtree and prefixing results with the mount target. Writes go through a `workspaceEdit` dispatcher that replaces the old `overlayEdit`, and `withChanges` rejects a changeset straddling a mount boundary rather than splitting it. The baseline is materialized by an internal `DoNotCache` `CacheVolume` field, so reads reflect the volume at call time while the resulting `Directory`'s content-derived digest still dedups downstream. **What's missing.** There are no tests across the four workspace types, so the write-through and persistence paths are unverified end to end. The baseline is copy-on-read rather than copy-on-write, export doesn't take a `LOCKED` share, and a whole-tree read doesn't shadow base content at a subtree mount. It sits at this position in the stack because the `workspaceEdit` refactor is what every later workspace change is written against — reverting it produces ten conflict regions across ~450 lines, several of which interleave mount code with commit-staging code.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: Trace reports as the result of a tool call
signal.text: An agent driving Dagger saw almost nothing of what it ran: a tool result was the return value plus a tail of log lines — enough to know a command failed, rarely why. The CLI's pretty final report already answers "what just happened", so render that as the tool result. A call whose span has descendants gets the rendered report; otherwise it stays on #13832's flat log path. `ReadTrace` joins the builtins, resolving a span, check name, or test name to the same rendering. A result carries the tool's own OUTPUT first (the byte guard drops the middle of an over-budget result), then the report — which is told to omit inline logs for exactly the spans OUTPUT claimed. **Scoping was the hard part**, and three bugs came out of it: reveal-independent surfacing assumed the whole trace as its root, so a report scoped to a tool call dropped every check it ran — the family now takes an explicit root; the replay provider emitted no tool-call display spans, so every LLM integration test exercised a shape production never produces; and `WalkSpans` inlined causal spans from other tool calls into scoped reports, which `StrictSubtree` closes. Successful reports also stopped dumping raw span trees — surfaced sections only, since OUTPUT plus the ReadLogs hint covers the rest. Rendering the `DB` is now cached per session and loaded incrementally — clientdb rows are append-only with monotonic IDs, making this a cursor problem rather than cache invalidation. Also here: agent-style report headings become a frontend opt instead of env sniffing, a `/span` console route reports one span's flags and parent chain, TESTS counts only leaf cases, nested transcript logs wrap at their rendered width, and multiline tool-call arg fallbacks collapse to one line.
signal.author: vito

signal.title: Services: discovery, trace surfacing, tool-log hygiene
signal.text: Services were easy to lose in a trace, and easy to drown in. **Discovery.** A service's logs hang off its exec span, reachable only via cause-purpose links — dagui followed them, clientdb didn't, so `ReadLogs` on the `asService` span returned nothing. clientdb now follows them too, and exec spans are marked `dagger.io/service` + hostname. `ListServices` closes the loop: each running service's hostname, ports, and span IDs, ready to feed into `ReadLogs`. `ReadLogs` itself recovers instead of dead-ending: an empty capture answers `(no logs beneath span X yet)` rather than erroring, the span argument accepts the forms agents actually paste (`span=<hex>`, `[traceparent:…]`), and out-of-range offsets or fruitless greps report how much data exists. **Surfacing.** Agent runs get a SERVICES section in the final report: hostname, command line, state, and a `span=<hex>` handle per instance, after the main rows. Agent-only on purpose — an agent may see nothing but the report, while a human already watched the service run in the tree. **Tool-log hygiene.** Three leaks into LLM tool results plugged: internal subtrees, whole service log histories, and raw SSE frames from nested LLM HTTP spans (hidden unless the request failed — then the bodies are the diagnosis). Tool logs are abridged by provenance, not position: the tool's own prints survive verbatim (with a 16 KiB backstop), and only nested output is trimmed to a tail behind a counted marker. Two fixes make that hold: Dang stdio now routes to the user-facing span (prints landed one hop too deep and were abridged away as build noise), and the internal filter only consults spans within the captured subtree (a cause-linked span's unrelated ancestors could silently hide logs).
signal.author: vito

signal.title: [backport-0.21] reduce e-graph contention and restore CI
signal.text: ## Summary Backports #13888 to the v0.21 maintenance line for v0.21.9 and includes the narrowly scoped compatibility fixes needed to validate that backport on the current CI/toolchain stack. Wide output equivalence classes made result removal repeatedly scan class digests and postings while holding `egraphMu`, causing superlinear release and metadata-prune work. The optimization adds an inverse output-class/result index and exact per-result posting bookkeeping while retaining conservative broad cleanup for imported state. Ownership, release cascades and callback order, lookup membership, expiry behavior, persistence compatibility, prune visibility, reset behavior, and the `egraphMu` lock domain remain unchanged. There is no persistence schema, API, or intended user-visible semantic change in the DagQL optimization. ## Source and scope - Source PR: #13888 - Main squash commit: `924f2b932a5e8517efca0a9f2205d5b7a288f67f` - Traceable optimization backport: `6c391620293f1821c32ae4be50438f1c968535b7` - Exact backport head: `be565e3d23a4b859f0840478d9c5ec5320de0709` - Target: `backport-0.21` for milestone v0.21.9 - Final range: four DCO-signed commits, 20 files The original optimization remains a focused nine-file backport: seven DagQL files retain the source patch IDs, and two architecture-doc hunks map mechanically from main's `internal-docs/` paths to the v0.21 `skills/cache-expert/references/` counterparts. No benchmark harness, runner, artifacts, implementation plan, benchmark-only documentation, schema change, or unrelated optimization is included. Three follow-up commits carry current-main fixes required by the v0.21 branch: 1. Remove `ReadHeaderTimeout` from all three unencrypted HTTP/2 servers, adapting main commit `b068d8a7be14b23b87a44854e428d17ea2330b48`. 2. Repair the `throttledGC` → `throttledSessionGC` test-field fallout left by the earlier production backport, and skip only the Java remote-module test whose development SDK version is unpublished (from `3755efceba33d4c59bd0e41beb640748dec4f0c7` and `ace77dd1af7c5044133677bdb9e34cc9b60c208a`). 3. Adapt the Helm/Wolfi package fix and docs from `4e37cc80cb6e92a347cd6f38510ceed31c42bece`, and inject the release module workspace as required when the current CLI regenerates it against a schema without `Query.currentWorkspace` (from `dac8f87c6af075158967a1250871a81bb2e2d2ed`). ## HTTP/2 failure diagnosis The old runtime shard was not a generic nested-engine cancellation. With Go 1.26.6, `net/http` applied `ReadHeaderTimeout` as a connection-level deadline to h2c connections and only disarmed it when `ReadTimeout > 0`. Every multiplexed nested-client stream therefore died at the configured 10-second boundary with `unexpected EOF`, followed by canceled codegen and exit 137. Removing that timeout from the three h2c servers is the exact main-branch fix. After the change, focused `TestGo/TestSignaturesUnexported` ran through the former cliff and passed in 34.730s (trace `2032b9130bd192832b2cd5f4c02add31`). The full module-runtime shard then passed every non-Elixir runtime. Its remaining Elixir failures explicitly report `OS monotonic time stepped backwards` before BEAM aborts with exit 134 (trace `d443fc462cc94b88b8da9c879e7283c7`), which is a separate host-clock failure rather than a hidden Dagger engine crash. ## Validation Compiled/test content at final head is identical to council-approved `b9ca3ee137f37d6b0b3bbc1fa3119c2c53935c6b`; the final amend adds only the Helm documentation hunk. signal.title: 1.0: better SDK UX
signal.text: ## Context In 1.0-beta, you manage Dagger SDKs directly from the command line. They are modules under the hood, but they have extra capabilities, so the CLI exposes them both as regular modules, and also in special commands. ## Problem The split between "SDK is a regular module" and "SDK has its own native commands" creates some confusion in the CLI. Specifically: ### SDK name vs. module name ```console # Accept a "SDK name", translate to a different "regular module name" under the hood $ dagger sdk install go # Don't accept the SDK name. User must guess the regular module name on their own $ dagger settings dagger-go-sdk ``` ### Round-trip of death First-time users must survive a round-trip from `dagger module` ("why can't I do anything") to `dagger sdk` ("what is a SDK and how do I get one") back to `dagger module` ("how do I use my SDK"). Then later, another round-trip: `dagger client` -> `dagger sdk` -> `dagger client` ```console # 1. Why can't I do anything? $ dagger module init --help # 2. What is a SDK and how do I get one $ dagger sdk search $ dagger sdk install FOO # 3. How do I use my SDK $ dagger module init FOO ``` ## Solution Fundamental design is sound. I propose cosmetic changes to reduce confusion: ### Frontend design Overview of the proposed change: | Action | Before | After | Note | | -- | -- | -- | -- | | Search for an SDK | `dagger sdk search` | `dagger search --sdk` | Use existing module search, with an optional filter | | Install an SDK | `dagger sdk install` | `dagger install` | Use existing module install. No new flag needed (SDKs are auto-detected) | | Uninstall an SDK | `dagger sdk uninstall` | `dagger uninstall` | Use existing module uninstall | | List installed SDKs (show SDK names) | `dagger sdk installed` | `dagger sdk -l` | Same pattern as `dagger check`, `dagger generate` etc | | Show information about an SDK | - | `dagger sdk info` | Useful to show module name, source, detected capabilities, etc | | Use an SDK to initialize a module | `dagger module init ` | `dagger sdk module init` | All things SDK under `dagger sdk`. No more `dagger module`! | | Use an SDK to remove and unclaim a module | - | `dagger sdk module remove` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to claim a module | - | `dagger sdk module claim` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to unclaim a module | - | `dagger sdk module unclaim` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to list claimed modules | - | `dagger sdk module claimed` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to list modules that *could* be claimed but are not | - | `dagger sdk module claimable` | This may require [backend support](#claimable-modules) | | Use an SDK to initialize a client | `dagger api client init ` | `dagger sdk client init` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to claim a client | - | `dagger sdk client claim` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to unclaim a client | - | `dagger sdk client unclaim` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to list claimed clients | - | `dagger sdk client claimed` | 👆 | | Use an SDK to list clients that *could* be claimed but are not | - | `dagger sdk client claimable` | This may require [backend support](#claimable-modules) | | Use an SDK to re-generate modules and/or clients | `dagger generate` | `dagger generate` | No change | Examples: ```console # Regular 'dagger install'. Note: no short name. $ dagger install github.com/dagger/go-sdk # 'dagger settings' is now 100% vanilla. If there is a name mismatch, it's not a SDK-specific problem $ dagger settings dagger-go-sdk # 'dagger sdk' for all things SDK. Explicit reference to module name. $ dagger sdk --help go Use the Go SDK (module: dagger-go-sdk) $ dagger sdk go --help module Develop Dagger modules, using the Go SDK client Generate clients to other Dagger modules, using the Go SDK $ dagger module module: no such command ``` ### Backend design Besides cosmetic reshuffling of commands, the main backend changes are the *SDK name*, and *SDK detection*. #### SDK name | | Before | After | | -- | -- | -- | | Who provides the SDK name? | The user at `sdk install` | The engine infers it as a convenience (`sdkName = moduleName.stripPrefix("dagger").stripSuffix("sdk").resolveConflicts())`. So `dagger-go-sdk` becomes `go`, and so on. | | Is the SDK name tied to builtin short names? | Yes | No: works the same for official and non-official SDKs | #### SDK detection | | Before | After | | -- | -- | -- | | How does the engine know it's installing an SDK? | The user says so: `dagger sdk install` | The engine checks each module for SDK capabilities: `initModule()` and `initClient()`. | #### Claimable modules This command may require a backend change. Perhaps new optional functions: `claimableModules()` and `claimableClients()` ?

signal.title: [backport-0.21] fix(engine): decouple active-clients API from session lifecycle locks
signal.text: ## Summary Backport #13542 to the v0.21 maintenance line for v0.21.9. The Cloud keeper polls `engine { clients }` as part of its composite heartbeat. On v0.21, that enumeration can block behind one session lifecycle lock held across initialization or teardown. Because the keeper does not publish until the query returns, one slow session can suppress all keeper heartbeats, make a live engine unschedulable, and eventually cause suspension. This backport decouples active-client observers from session lifecycle work while preserving the complete synchronization redesign from the source fix. ## Source - Source PR: https://github.com/dagger/dagger/pull/13542 - Source commit: https://github.com/dagger/dagger/commit/0e21927e46c97a7ccb80670d6353d603e95c2885 - Applied with `cherry-pick -x` onto `origin/backport-0.21` at `9f68624bf69c23c01861e298651656ecac780285` - The v0.21 concurrency prerequisite from #13474 is already present as `cd9c80b9da99c0a90126b4a999400543f110c322` ## v0.21 adaptation The main-only `wcprofEnabled` field from #13393 does not exist on v0.21 and is not a dependency, so the conflict-only field and assignment were omitted. This is not a reduced `Clients` unlock. It retains the full semantic unit: - immutable session identity before registry publication - atomic lifecycle state - lifecycle-only mutex - lock-free `Clients`, `activeClientIDs`, and `clientFromIDs` observers - client publication only after successful initialization - removed tombstones and pointer-conditional registry deletion - client DB opening outside `clientMu` - graceful-stop session snapshot - all source liveness/race regressions adapted to v0.21 ## Validation Passed: - `gofmt -w engine/server/server.go engine/server/session.go engine/server/session_test.go` - `go test ./engine/server -run "^(TestClientsDoesNotBlockWhileSessionLifecycleLocked|TestActiveClientIDsDoesNotBlockWhileSessionLifecycleLocked|TestGetOrInitClientReturnsFastForRemovedTombstone|TestClientFromIDsStateGating|TestSessionLifecycleObserverConcurrency)$" -count=1` - `go test ./engine/server` - `go test -race ./engine/server` - `git diff --check origin/backport-0.21...HEAD` ## Release note Adds `.changes/unreleased/Fixed-20260810-150651.yaml` for v0.21.9, attributed to source PR #13542. Cloud-side per-operation deadlines remain separate follow-up work and are not changed by this backport.

signal.title: withServiceBinding: a service with a custom hostname is unresolvable when another module started it first
signal.text: ## Summary `Container.withServiceBinding` fails at hosts-file setup — before the user's command runs — when the bound service has a **custom hostname** (`Service.withHostname`) and was **first started by a different module** than the one doing the binding: ``` lookup my-svc-host for hosts file: lookup my-svc-host on 10.87.0.1:53: no such host lookup my-svc-host.<modhash>.<sesshash>.dagger.local on 10.87.0.1:53: no such host lookup my-svc-host.<sesshash>.dagger.local on 10.87.0.1:53: no such host ``` This affects **any** `*Service` with a custom hostname that crosses a module boundary — as a returned value, a field on a returned object, or a function argument. It is not specific to any one service type. The failure is **ordering-dependent in a way user code cannot work around**: whichever module first starts the service owns its DNS domain, and the other participant can then never resolve it. A module that needs to talk to its own service before handing it to a caller (register a schema, seed a topic, run a migration, warm a cache) breaks the caller; keeping the service up from the caller's side instead breaks the module. There is no ordering that satisfies both. ## Reproduction Two modules. The producer creates a service with a custom hostname, **starts it**, and returns it; the consumer binds it and execs. **`producer/main.go`** (`dagger.json`: `{"name": "producer", "sdk": {"source": "go"}}`) ```go package main import ( "context" "dagger/producer/internal/dagger" ) type Producer struct{} type Registry struct { Svc *dagger.Service Hostname string } // Serve starts the service before returning it. Starting module-side is the trigger. func (m *Producer) Serve(ctx context.Context) (*Registry, error) { const hostname = "started-registry-host" svc := dag.Container(). From("busybox:1.37.0"). WithWorkdir("/srv"). WithNewFile("index.html", "hello from the producer"). WithDefaultArgs([]string{"httpd", "-v", "-f"}). WithExposedPort(80). AsService(). WithHostname(hostname) if _, err := svc.Start(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err } return &Registry{Svc: svc, Hostname: hostname}, nil } ``` **`main.go`** (`dagger.json`: `{"name": "consumer", "sdk": {"source": "go"}, "dependencies": [{"name": "producer", "source": "producer"}]}`) ```go package main import ( "context" "fmt" ) type Consumer struct{} func (m *Consumer) Run(ctx context.Context) error { reg := dag.Producer().Serve() hostname, err := reg.Hostname(ctx) if err != nil { return err } resp, err := dag.Container(). From("busybox:1.37.0"). WithServiceBinding(hostname, reg.Svc()). WithExec([]string{"wget", "-O-", "http://" + hostname}). Stdout(ctx) if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to reach bound service: %w", err) } if resp != "hello from the producer" { return fmt.Errorf("unexpected response: %q", resp) } return nil } ``` ``` dagger call run ``` **Actual:** fails with `lookup started-registry-host for hosts file: ... no such host`. **Expected:** the bound alias resolves and the exec succeeds. Removing the `svc.Start(ctx)` from the producer makes it pass — the binding then starts the service itself, in the consumer's domain. ## Root cause 1. **A custom hostname is namespaced into the domain of whichever module starts the service.** `Service.startContainer` (`core/service.go`) keys the domain off `query.ModuleParent(ctx)` — the *calling client*, not the module that authored the service: ```go if mod, err := query.ModuleParent(ctx); err == nil && svc.CustomHostname != "" { domain = network.ModuleDomain(modDigest, clientMetadata.SessionID) ... } else { domain = network.SessionDomain(clientMetadata.SessionID) } fullHost := host + "." + domain ``` 2. **That FQDN is the only name registered.** It becomes the service container's hostname, is passed to CNI as `K8S_POD_NAME`, and the `dnsname` plugin writes a single `ip⇥FQDN` line into dnsmasq's `addn-hosts`. `cniprovider` never populates the declared `aliases` capability, so there are no CNAMEs and no second record. dnsmasq runs `local=/dagger.local/`, making anything else under that domain an authoritative NXDOMAIN. 3. **The consuming exec searches only its own module domain plus the session domain** (`core/container_exec.go`, `engine/engineutil/executor_spec.go`), and resolves each binding from its **bare** hostname. Those are exactly the three lookups in the error. 4. **`ServiceKey` has no domain component** (`core/services.go`), so a service already started by the producer is warm-joined verbatim by the consumer — `svc.Start` never re-runs, and the domain is never renegotiated. So the consumer ends up holding a perfectly valid handle to a *running* service whose only registered name it cannot resolve. ### Why it looks intermittent - With several bindings, the hosts-file loop iterates a Go map (`execMD.HostAliases`), so which alias is reported first varies between runs. - `Detach` reaps a zero-refcount service after `DetachGracePeriod` (10s); a later bind of a fully-reaped service restarts it and recomputes the domain, which *succeeds* — but against a fresh, empty service. If the producer called `Service.start()`, the refcount is pinned for the session (`StartResultWithOpts` discards the release closure) and the failure is deterministic. ## Is this intended? `Service.withHostname` deliberately namespaces custom hostnames per-module (#8641: *"a hostname … which will be automatically namespaced within the module"*), and `TestWithHostnameModuleScoping` asserts the bare-DNS half of that on purpose — a module's custom hostname is *not* reachable across modules. But that test never calls `withServiceBinding`, and I think that's the gap. Binding is an **explicit capability the consumer already holds** — it was handed the service deliberately — so it seems different in kind from ambient bare-hostname DNS. A service without a custom hostname (session domain) already works across modules in exactly this shape, as `TestContentAddressedModuleScoping` shows. If the maintainers consider the current behavior intended, then this is instead a feature request: there's no way for a producing module to publish a service its callers can reach, and `withHostname` is unusable for services whose hostname must be baked into config before the container is built (`advertised.listeners`, virtual-host routing, TLS SANs). ## Related surfaces (same root cause) - `DNSConfig` (`core/git_remote.go`) installs only the session domain, so module-scoped services are invisible to the git / http / registry binding paths regardless of who started them. - `ModuleParent` walks the client parent chain while the exec's `CurrentModule` does not, so a nested-exec client can start a service in module M's domain while its own execs get no module domain at all — same failure, no cross-module handoff needed. ## Environment - Reproduced on `main` @ `d4cd0707` (v1.0.0-beta.8) and originally hit on v0.21.7. - Linux, x86_64. ## Origin Surfaced in [z5labs/devex#147](https://github.com/z5labs/devex/issues/147), where a Kafka module hands brokers and a Schema Registry to a consumer container. Filing here generalized, since it turned out to have nothing to do with Schema Registry specifically. The real-world repro ([z5labs/devex#153](https://github.com/z5labs/devex/pull/153)) fails on the broker alias or the registry alias nondeterministically, depending only on map ordering. I have a fix with regression tests working locally (record the FQDN the running service registered under, prefer it when building the hosts file, leave bare-hostname scoping untouched — existing scoping tests stay green, and the devex repro goes green end-to-end). Happy to open a PR, but wanted to check the intended-behavior question above first, since that determines whether the fix belongs in the binding path or in a new API.

signal.title: sdk(improvement): support nullable object returns
signal.text: #### What Support nullable GraphQL object and interface results in generated clients and module SDKs. Nullable methods now resolve the object's ID before returning. A missing ID becomes the language's empty value; a present ID is rebuilt as a normal client. Non-null object methods stay lazy. #### Client APIs Each SDK uses its normal optional value: `Nullable` in Go, `null` in TypeScript, PHP, and .NET, `None` in Python, `Option` in Rust, `Optional` in Java, and `{:ok, value | nil}` in Elixir. For example, Go callers can handle `GitCommit.releaseTag` explicitly: ```go result, err := commit.ReleaseTag(ctx) if err != nil { return err } tag, ok := result.Get() if !ok { return nil } name, err := tag.Name(ctx) ``` #### Module APIs Module authors can declare nullable object returns with their SDK's existing syntax: - TypeScript: `Promise<User | null>` - PHP: `?Directory` - Java: `Optional<Directory>` - Go: `dagger.Nullable[*dagger.Directory]` - Python: `User | None` - Elixir: `User.t() | nil` Rust and .NET do not currently support modules. Dang already supports nullable return types. #### Compatibility and tests Generated templates use the schema version to keep the old lazy method shape before `v1.0.0-beta.10`. From beta.10 onward, nullable object methods use the resolved optional result. Tests cover both sides of the version boundary, object and interface results, and both present and null module returns. Java and .NET also exercise the runtime null path directly.

signal.title: stdlib: remove dependency on polyfill module
signal.text: ## Problem Our official modules import a "polyfill" module for features that want in the engine, but didn't have the patience to wait for :) At 1.0 launch, the number of official modules that import polyfill should be ideally zero, or at most a very small number for niche use cases. As it stands today, aspiring module developers that peek at our own modules, will undoubtebly have to learn about polyfill, which will make their learning and development journey more complicated. ## Solution Remove all dependencies on github.com/dagger/polyfill (and legacy github.com/dagger/sdk-sdk/polyfill) in all modules under github.com/dagger

signal.title: Remove github.com URLs from official modules
signal.text: ## Context Dagger 1.0 has "official modules": modules developed and maintained by the Dagger team. They are a core part of the user experience: you are strongly expected, and encouraged, to use at least one in your Dagger setup. ## Problem Like all other modules, official modules are referenced by their git repository URL. There is no special shorthand or alias. Since they are hosted in github, they are referenced by URLs in the github.com domain. For example: ```console $ dagger install github.com/dagger/go $ dagger install github.com/dagger/python ``` With the rapid unraveling of Github's uptime and reputation, and the erosion of its monopoly over git hosting, it no longer makes sense to tie ourselves to the Github brand in this way. We need a safety buffer to insulate ourselves. ## Solution Either introduce "short names", similar to Docker's official images, or stick to DNS and use a domain that we use, and can redirect later. ### Option 1: short names ```console $ dagger install go $ dagger install python ``` ### Option 2: independent domain ```console $ dagger install dagger.io/go $ dagger install dagger.io/python ```
signal.author: shykes

signal.title: fix: accept @ and # in git refs
signal.text: Git refs used different separators depending on where they appeared: - Module sources accepted `@ref`, but not `#ref`. - Git-backed directory and file arguments accepted `#ref`, but not `@ref`. This PR makes both forms work everywhere. Users can now write either separator in `dagger.toml` module sources and in directory or file settings, and copy a Git URL between them without changing it. Includes a workspace regression test that loads a module source using `#ref` and reads a directory setting using `@ref`. Tests: - `go test ./util/gitutil -run '^TestParseURL$'` - `go test ./core -run '^TestParseRefString$' -count=1` - `dagger --x-release=v1.0.0-beta.9 api call engine-dev test --pkg ./core/integration --run='TestWorkspace/TestWorkspaceModuleSettingsRuntime/git_refs_accept_the_same_separators_in_sources_and_settings'` Fixes #13856

signal.title: docs: clarify GOPROXY requires custom engine SYSTEMENV
signal.text: ## Summary Clarify the Service Proxies docs for `_DAGGER_ENGINE_SYSTEMENV_GOPROXY`: show the custom-engine path that actually works, and call out the two setups that don't (host-only SYSTEMENV, plain `GOPROXY` on the engine). Related to #13596. ## What I started from #13596: in a network where `proxy.golang.org` is blocked, Python module load dies in codegen `go get`. The reporter set `_DAGGER_ENGINE_SYSTEMENV_GOPROXY` on the host and plain `GOPROXY` on the engine — still hit Google. First question I had: is codegen hardwired to Google, or is the setting just never reaching it? Looking at the history (#6599 → #7255 → #9362 → #10962) shaped that. This isn't a new China feature request. Dagger already built a Go-proxy escape hatch; the contract was always custom engine + `_DAGGER_ENGINE_SYSTEMENV_GOPROXY`. #9362 was the same confusion (plain `GOPROXY` expected to work) and got closed as "supported, underdocumented." So I stopped treating "codegen ignores everything" as the first assumption and tested **wiring** instead. ## What I tested Couldn't become a China network, so I didn't try to reproduce the exact `i/o timeout`. Instead I pointed the proxy at a dead address (`http://127.0.0.1:1`): - if codegen uses my setting → fail talking to `127.0.0.1:1` - if it ignores me → still talk to Google Results on v0.21.7 (same idea checked on v0.21.8 for the bad paths): 1. Custom engine + `_DAGGER_ENGINE_SYSTEMENV_GOPROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1` → `connection refused` to `127.0.0.1:1`. Setting reaches codegen. 2. Same SYSTEMENV only on the host → auto-started engine has no GOPROXY/SYSTEMENV. Matches the issue. 3. Plain `GOPROXY=http://127.0.0.1:1` on the engine → codegen still succeeds via Google. Ignored. Matches the issue. ## What I think this means Not "codegen can never use a mirror." More: the knobs people actually turn don't land in codegen, so it falls back to Google and *feels* hardwired. The docs already said "custom engine," but not how, and not what fails. That's the gap. ## What this PR changes On `docs/current_docs/reference/configuration/proxy.mdx`: - spell out custom engine + `_DAGGER_ENGINE_SYSTEMENV_GOPROXY` with a concrete example - warn that host-only SYSTEMENV and plain `GOPROXY` don't work Based on the tests above, not on changing engine behavior. ## Testing Docs-only. Reconfirmed the working path: dead SYSTEMENV on a custom engine → codegen dials `127.0.0.1:1`. Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)
signal.author: EmmS21

signal.title: dagql: reduce e-graph result-removal contention
signal.text: ## Motivation Removing a result from a wide output equivalence class repeatedly scanned the class's digests and result postings while holding `egraphMu`. Release and metadata-prune work therefore grew superlinearly as the class widened, increasing lock contention for unrelated cache operations. ## Design This change adds three cache-owned derived indexes: - an inverse output-equivalence-class-to-results index; - an exact per-result digest-posting index; and - an exact/broad posting classification for result cleanup. Newly published results record their exact digest postings. Imported results remain conservatively broad because the persistence schema does not contain exact result/term memberships. Broad imported cleanup therefore retains the safe class-posting scan; this change does not claim to remove that scan. The inverse output-class index replaces the separate deterministic class-wide survivor scan with an expiry-aware lookup over associated results. ## Correctness and compatibility Forward and inverse output-class associations are maintained as a pair across publication, merge, compaction, import, expiry, reset, and rollback. Merge and compaction canonicalize roots and rebuild the paired indexes together. Posting insertion and removal use a centralized exact/broad classification, and the survivor predicate preserves expiry behavior. Ownership counts, release cascades and callback order, lookup candidate membership, release/prune visibility, tracing and mutation order, prune cadence, and the `egraphMu` lock domain remain unchanged. Reset clears all three indexes with the e-graph. There is no persistence schema, version, migration, API, or user-visible semantic change. Import reconstructs result/output-equivalence-class associations and marks imported postings broad. Exact result/term associations remain unavailable after import, so the existing conservative class-scan fallback is preserved. No changie entry is included because this is internal derived bookkeeping with no user-facing API or semantic change. ## Scope and history The final merge diff is nine files: three production files, four focused correctness-test files, and two existing architecture documents. It contains the production optimization and its regression coverage, without benchmark infrastructure or a PR-only implementation plan. The eleven-commit branch history retains the reviewed empirical and planning work for provenance. The final `dagql: remove e-graph benchmark scaffolding` commit removes every benchmark-only test, fixture, observer, artifact helper, runner script, and benchmark/plan document from the merge tree. The two implementation commits remain separate conceptual review and rollback boundaries. ## Validation The final rebased head `8bfba77e77` passed: - `go test ./dagql -count=1` — 1.872s - `go test -race ./dagql -count=1` — 4.161s - the 14 focused affected DagQL tests — 0.865s - `dagger check golang:lint-all` - `dagger check markdown-lint:lint` - `dagger check golang:generate-all` - `dagger check markdown-lint:fix` - `gofmt` and `git diff --check` All eleven commits carry one matching DCO signoff. The rebased implementation commits retain the stable patch IDs of the reviewed originals, and the final production/docs patch is identical after removing benchmark-only instrumentation. The merge diff contains no generated/schema change. ## Paired benchmark evidence The measurements were collected with the reviewed development harness that is intentionally removed by the final cleanup commit. The measured production implementation is unchanged in the final merge diff; the evidence binds to that production behavior, not to final-tree or rebuilt-binary identity. - Transient wide release: R256 improved from 46.318 ms to 2.356 ms and R512 from 181.319 ms to 5.379 ms. The timing slope changed from 3.91x to 2.28x, while allocation scaling per doubling changed from 3.94x to 1.99x. - Persisted-fresh prune: R256 improved from 20.256 ms to 5.540 ms and R512 from 156.145 ms to 12.378 ms. The 12.6x R512 ratio and 7.709x baseline timing slope are host-specific, not expected production factors. The stronger structural result is allocation scaling per doubling changing from 3.86x to 1.98x. - Imported release R256 improved from 86.020 ms to 19.765 ms while retaining all 263,683 broad postings. Broad posting cleanup remains; the gain comes from removing the separate class-wide survivor scan. Allocations changed from 1,769,611 to 1,031. - The independent 50,000-result control produced candidate 317.357 ms, baseline 277.558 ms, and the one bounded candidate repeat 270.377 ms. No control regression was demonstrated at this measurement precision; none was excluded. Identical allocations/bytes, within-2% RSS, and matching fixture/posting/lock counters support treating the first candidate point as noise rather than claiming a speedup. Every process exited successfully, ran one exact sample, reported zero dropped observations, and preserved fixture, prune, and lock-counter populations. Only the allowed noisy control arm was repeated once. The same-host paired comparison was explicitly authorized because the original Linux VM was unstable. Host-specific timing factors are not production guarantees; the near-linear allocation scaling is the stronger evidence that the quadratic removal term is gone. Raw outputs and SHA-256 manifests are retained internally. ## Rollback and non-goals The two implementation commits are conceptual rollback boundaries: first the output-class inverse index, then exact posting tracking and cleanup. This slice does not add lock sharding, tombstones, asynchronous cleanup, persistence-schema changes, exact imported association persistence, ownership-semantic changes, imported read-path redesign, or broader e-graph optimization.

signal.author: shykes

signal.title: How do we support workspace configs that arent at the repo root
signal.text: Related issues: - https://github.com/dagger/dagger/pull/13890 - https://github.com/dagger/dagger/pull/13892 - https://github.com/dagger/dagger/pull/13893 - https://github.com/dagger/dagger/pull/13882 We currently have a few assumptions that the Workspace config (dagger.toml) is at the repository root. At one point in the Workspace design, we talked about nested Workspace configs, but that was cut for now because of the complexity it adds. The question is, if we do support dagger.toml placed somewhere other than the repo root, how do we support that - How does Cloud Checks determine the correct config location? - If there are multiple configs, how do we select one? - Are paths in the config always from the repo root or workspace config?
signal.author: kpenfound

signal.title: fix(check): align @check with @generate on required arguments
signal.text: `@up`, `@generate` and `@agent` all refuse to load a module whose marked function demands an argument the caller never supplies. `@check` didn't, so the same mistake showed up as one fewer entry in `dagger check -l` — indistinguishable from a check that passed, while `dagger functions` still listed the function. Before: ``` $ dagger functions needs-arg A @check with a required argument runnable A check a rollup can run $ dagger check -l my-module:runnable ← needs-arg is simply gone, no warning ``` After, matching what `@generate` already does: ``` $ dagger check -l ✘ ERROR object "MyModule" function "needsArg" is marked @check but declares required argument "name"; @check functions must be callable with no arguments ``` **Scope.** One validator plus its dispatch, mirroring `validateGeneratorFunction`. No return-type constraint — unlike `@up`/`@generate`, a check reports itself however it likes (`Void`, an error, a `Container` to run). An auto-injected `Workspace!` is not a caller-supplied argument, so checks taking one keep loading; there's a fixture pinning that. **Compatibility.** A module with a `@check` that declares a required argument now fails to load instead of quietly losing that check. Verified against this repo and its published dependencies: `dagger check -l` lists the same 84 checks before and after (`ci:bootstrap` takes `source: Workspace!`, `python-client:lint` takes `paths` with a default — both unaffected). **Testing.** `dagger api call engine-dev test --pkg ./core/integration --run='^TestChecks$|^TestGenerators$|^TestUp$|^TestAgents$'` → 213 passed, 0 failed. New `TestChecksValidationRejectsRequiredArg` covers both the rejection and the Workspace-argument case, alongside the existing `badgenerate-arg`/`badup-arg` tests. **Not included.** A check whose *owning object* is only reachable through a function that requires an argument (`suite(name: String!): Suite!`) is still silently dropped from rollups. Making that a load error was tried and rejected: `github.com/dagger/go` has exactly that shape (`GoModule.lint` behind `module(path:)`), so it would break `dagger check` for this repo and every user of that module. Surfacing it needs a warning rather than an error, which is left for a follow-up.

Release notes

Sourced from github.com/99designs/gqlgen's releases.

v0.17.94

Upcoming Potentially Breaking Changes Warning

This release has changes in the Federation plugin, introducing opt-in changes that will become the default in the next release (v0.17.95).

When configured, the federation plugin creates an entity resolver that accepts a list of representations, improving performance by reducing the number of individual resolver calls.

// IMPORTANT: The output slice order is critical and must match the input slice order exactly! func (r *entityResolver) FindUserByIDs(ctx context.Context, reps []*entity.UserByIDsInput) ([]*model.User, error) { output := make([]*model.User, len(reps)) for i, user := range reps { output[i] = &model.User{ ID: user.ID, Name: "User " + user.ID, } } 
return output, nil 
 
}

The @entityResolver directive enables optimization for entity resolver generation in GraphQL federation, and can be opted in by specifying multi: true as in:

type MultiHello @key(fields: "name") @entityResolver(multi: true)

Or you can enable this feature by default by setting the federation.options.entity_resolver_multi flag in your configuration:

federation: filename: graph/federation.go package: graph version: 2 options: entity_resolver_multi: true

Release 0.4.0

1Password Go SDK v0.4.0

NEW

  • Desktop App integration: The SDK can now authenticate via an authorization prompt from the 1Password app.
  • Vault CRUDL: You can now fully manage 1Password vaults with the SDK, including creating, reading, updating, deleting and listing.
  • Vault group permission management operations: You can now grant, update and revoke group access to vaults using grantGroupPermissions, updateGroupPermissions, and revokeGroupPermissions functions.
  • Item batch management: You can now retrieve, create, update and delete items in batch, enabling more scalable item management.

1Password Go SDK v0.4.0-beta.2

FIXED

  • Handling locked 1Password app state: When the 1Password app gets locked after the SDK client is authenticated, it will now automatically re-authenticate.

Updates `github.com/99designs/gqlgen` from 0.17.89 to 0.17.94
Release notes

Sourced from github.com/99designs/gqlgen's releases.

v0.17.94

Upcoming Potentially Breaking Changes Warning

This release has changes in the Federation plugin, introducing opt-in changes that will become the default in the next release (v0.17.95).

When configured, the federation plugin creates an entity resolver that accepts a list of representations, improving performance by reducing the number of individual resolver calls.

// IMPORTANT: The output slice order is critical and must match the input slice order exactly! func (r *entityResolver) FindUserByIDs(ctx context.Context, reps []*entity.UserByIDsInput) ([]*model.User, error) { output := make([]*model.User, len(reps)) for i, user := range reps { output[i] = &model.User{ ID: user.ID, Name: "User " + user.ID, } } 
return output, nil 
 
}

The @entityResolver directive enables optimization for entity resolver generation in GraphQL federation, and can be opted in by specifying multi: true as in:

type MultiHello @key(fields: "name") @entityResolver(multi: true)

Or you can enable this feature by default by setting the federation.options.entity_resolver_multi flag in your configuration:

federation: filename: graph/federation.go package: graph version: 2 options: entity_resolver_multi: true

experimental/v0.221.0

0.221.0

:boom: Breaking Changes

  • feat(sdk-logs)!: configure the force flush timeout per call #6931 @​LarryHu0217
    • (user-facing): LoggerProviderOptions.forceFlushTimeoutMillis has been removed; pass timeoutMillis to LoggerProvider.forceFlush() instead.
  • feat(instrumentation-http)!: emit only stable HTTP semantic conventions. The OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN environment variable no longer changes HTTP attribute or metric emission — old (v1.7.0) and duplicate (http/http/dup) semconv outputs have been removed. #6819 @​maryliag
  • feat(instrumentation-fetch)!: emit only stable HTTP semantic conventions. The semconvStabilityOptIn instrumentation config option has been removed; old (v1.7.0) and duplicate semconv outputs are no longer emitted. #6819 @​maryliag
  • feat(instrumentation-xml-http-request)!: emit only stable HTTP semantic conventions. The semconvStabilityOptIn instrumentation config option has been removed; old (v1.7.0) and duplicate semconv outputs are no longer emitted. #6819 @​maryliag
  • feat(instrumentation-grpc)!: emit only stable network semantic conventions. The OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN environment variable no longer changes attribute emission — net.peer.name and net.peer.port (old) are no longer set; only server.address and server.port (stable). #6819 @​maryliag

:rocket: Features

  • feat(sdk-logs): allow modifying ReadWriteLogRecord properties (including hrTime, hrTimeObserved, and spanContext) in accordance with the OpenTelemetry Logs specification #6923 @​Babul422
  • feat(sdk-node): emit a deprecation warning when the JaegerPropagator is selected via OTEL_PROPAGATORS or declarative config; use tracecontext instead. @​pichlermarc
  • feat(instrumentation-http): set error.type to status code in metrics for error requests. #6919 @​raphael-theriault-swi

experimental/v0.220.0

0.220.0

:boom: Breaking Changes

  • refactor(sdk-logs)!: refactor BatchLogRecordProcessor constructor signature #6817 @​trentm
    • (user-facing): BatchLogRecordProcessor now takes a single options object with all possible properties, instead of two separate arguments. For example, before new BatchLogRecordProcessor(exporter, { maxQueueSize: 1000 }), after new BatchLogRecordProcessor({ exporter, maxQueueSize: 1000 }).
    • interface BufferConfig -> interface BatchLogRecordProcessorOptions, and now includes the exporter property
    • interface BatchLogRecordProcessorBrowserConfig -> interface BatchLogRecordProcessorBrowserOptions
    • (user-facing): SimpleLogRecordProcessor now takes a single options object with all possible properties. For example, before new SimpleLogRecordProcessor(exporter), after new SimpleLogRecordProcessor({ exporter }). #6836
  • refactor(configuration)!: change config file parsing to not add default values, nor merge *_list fields #6765 @​trentm
    • Responsibility for handling declarative config "nullBehavior" and "defaultBehavior" belongs in the "create" handling, currently in the "sdk-node" package.
  • docs(shim-opencensus): Notice: The @opentracing/shim-opencensus package will be removed in SDK 3.x, planned for approximately September 2026.
    • The OpenCensus and OpenTracing compatibility requirements in the OpenTelemetry specification have been deprecated.
  • chore(sdk-node)!: Drop support for deprecated OpenCensusMetricProducer from declarative config

:rocket: Features

  • feat(configuration): bump config schema to v1.1.0; rename without_scope_info → scope_info_enabled and without_target_info/development → target_info_enabled/development on the Prometheus pull exporter (semantics inverted), rename with_resource_constant_labels → resource_constant_labels. Validate file_format per the configuration versioning spec: accept any minor version of major 1 (e.g. 1.0, 1.1), warn when the minor version is newer than supported, and reject other major versions. #6781 @​MikeGoldsmith
  • feat(sdk-node): wire up id_generator from declarative config #6782 @​MikeGoldsmith
  • feat(sdk-node): wire up tracer_provider.sampler from declarative config (always_on, always_off, trace_id_ratio_based, parent_based); unrecognized variants warn and fall back to ParentBased(AlwaysOn) #6506 @​MikeGoldsmith
  • feat(propagator-env-carrier): empty name normalization #6827 @​pellared
  • feat(propagator-env-carrier): make EnvironmentGetter read the current process.env #6853 @​pellared

  • fix(sdk-logs): stop Logger.emit() doing work (record construction, metrics, processor onEmit) after the LoggerProvider has shut down #6826 @​anneheartrecord
  • fix(sdk-node): pass all config properties (endpoint, headers, timeout, TLS, compression, temporality preference, default histogram aggregation) to OTLP metric exporters in declarative config #6814 @​MikeGoldsmith
  • fix(sdk-logs): default BatchLogRecordProcessor scheduleDelayMillis is 1000 #6796 @​trentm
  • fix(configuration): percent-decode keys and values in resource.attributes_list per spec #6787 @​MikeGoldsmith
  • fix(configuration): default log_level to info in env-based config initialization for consistency with file-based config #6788 @​MikeGoldsmith

signal.title: 🐞 `0.21.0` has broken Python modules with `git` dependencies
signal.text: ### What is the issue? I am trying to add a `git` dependency to my modules' `pyproject.toml`: ```toml [tool.uv.sources] dagger-io = { path = "sdk", editable = true } pytest-otel = { git = "https://github.com/dagger/pytest.git", subdirectory = "pytest_otel", rev = "main" } ``` this works fine with `0.20.8`, but doesn't work with `0.21.0`, I think it breaks module introspection. `dagger functions` is already failing. ### Dagger version dagger v0.21.0 (image://registry.dagger.io/engine:v0.21.0) darwin/arm64/v8 ### Steps to reproduce Add any git dependency to the module's `pyproject.toml` ### Log output ``` › dagger functions ✔ connect 0.3s ✘ load workspace: . 3.3s ERROR ┇ loading type definitions › load module: daggerverse-core › ModuleSource.asModule(legacyNameOverride: "daggerverse-core") › load dep modules › ModuleSource.asModule › ✘ asModule getModDef 0.1s ERROR Using CPython 3.14.3 interpreter at: /usr/local/bin/python3.14 Updating https://github.com/dagger/pytest.git (main) × Failed to download and build `pytest-otel @ │ git+https://github.com/dagger/pytest.git@main#subdirectory=pytest_otel` ├─▶ Git operation failed ╰─▶ Git executable not found. Ensure that Git is installed and available. ! failed to call module "ts-dagger-module" to get functions: call constructor: exit code: 1 ```
